replying_to: Replying to One-shot Conditional Sampling: MMD meets Nearest Neighbors
display_title: Official Review of Submission15928 by Reviewer k7GW

summary.value: The paper proposes a conditional sampling method based on maximum mean discrepancies. To this end, the authors introduce a conditioning variable into MMD-GANs and minimize the expected MMD of the approximated and true posterior distribution. Here, the MMD is discretized based on a nearest neighbor search. From a theoretical side the paper proves a bound how the restriction of the generator to be a neural network effects the minimal objective value and shows some convergence result of the discrete estimator. Numerical examples are performed on MNIST and CelebA for superresolution and denoising.

strengths.value: The paper is generally sound in the sense that the generative model actually minimizes a distance to the target which can generally be evaluated. Also it considers the approximation class of neural networks instead of just assuming that neural networks are universal function approximators.

weaknesses.value:
Major:

- Literature: Conditional sampling or generative modeling by directly minimizing the MMD have previously been considered in the context of gradient flows in [1,2,3,4]. In particular [2] considers the exact same problem and proves corresponding error bounds. The authors should rework the literature part and maybe compare to [2].

- Generally the optimal sampler $\bar g$ is neither unique nor regular. Plenty of works show that the Lipschitz constant (and thus also the modulus of continuity) must explode whenever we approximate multimodal or heavy-tailed distributions, see e.g. [5,6]. In practice, the bound from Thm 4.1 will be very very loose. Also, the notation is a bit confusing as the definition of $\omega_{\bar g}$ skips one of the arguments of $\bar g$ (I guess it is the conditioning which is omitted here).

- There is a significant mismatch between minimizing the MMD and its empirical estimators, in the sense that one needs a very large batch size in order to approximate the MMD precisely. Using a minibatch approximation usually yields blurred results which can be seen very well in Figure 2 where the CGMMD produces plenty of samples outside of the support of the target distribution compared to the baselines. A discussion on this topic is missing.

- Experiments: Compared to the literature, the paper only considers quite small experiments. I am not sure, whether denoising or superresolution tasks on MNIST really make sense as it is a really simplistic dataset. The quality of the results seems to be below classical image reconstruction methods like total variation. Also, for this kind of task the evaluation of FID and inception score does not make sense, as they have a predefined ground truth and metrics like PSNR, SSIM or LPIPS can cover them much better (I noted that PSNR and SSIM are reported, but my point is that it doesn't really make sense to report FID and IS in this case). Given that the method matches the distributions of a generator with a data distribution, the authors should evaluate how much generative power their model has. Suitable tasks could be class conditional sampling or box-inpainting.

Minor: 

- Typo: In Thm 4.1 in the definition of $\omega_{\bar g}$ there is missing the bar within the sup.

- I would prefer if the authors sharpened their Contributions section a bit to showcase what is new and what is taken from the literature. If I understand it correctly, the definition of the ECMMD and its empirical computation via neighborhood graphs comes from the literature, while the contribution in this paper is the construction of a conditional MMD GAN.

- Please state some relevant information about the experiments in Section 5. E.g. which kernel is used, which batch size etc.

- Citations are not always accurate. For instance the fact that $P_{Y|X}=P_{Z|X}$ almost surely iff $P_{Y,X}=P_{Z,X}$ (line 97 to 101 and Lemma 2.1) is simply Bayes theorem and that the corresponding metrics are zero is an immediate consequence and existance of the mapping $\bar g$ already follows from Breniers theorem; the citations in the paper are far away from being the origin of these results. Similarly, the form of the MMD in (2.2) exists for decades in the literature and attributing it to Chatterjee et al. is inaccurate.

---

[1] Maximum mean discrepancy gradient flow, NeurIPS 2019

[2] Posterior Sampling Based on Gradient Flows of the MMD with Negative Distance Kernel, ICLR 2024

[3] Generative Sliced MMD Flows with Riesz Kernels, ICLR 2024

[4] Deep MMD gradient flow without adversarial training, ICLR 2025

[5] Tails of Lipschitz triangular flows, ICML 2020

[6] Can push-forward generative models fit multimodal distributions?, NeurIPS 2022

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for a careful reading of the manuscript and an insightful detailed review. Below, we address the reviewer's questions and concerns.

> Literature: Conditional sampling or generative modeling by directly minimizing the MMD have previously been considered in the context of gradient flows in [1,2,3,4]. In particular [2] considers the exact same problem and proves corresponding error bounds. The authors should rework the literature part and maybe compare to [2].

We thank the reviewer for suggesting the literature on MMD-based gradient flows. We have included a discussion in the Appendix A of the revised manuscript. We also appreciate the reviewer for pointing out the work [13]. While this work addresses the same problem of conditional sample generation from the perspective of Bayesian inverse problems, it differs from our approach in two primary ways. First, their method is based on gradient flows, which represents a different approach to learning distributions. Second, they consider only a fixed choice of kernel, the negative distance kernel, whereas our approach allows greater flexibility in the choice of kernels. Additionally we believe that in terms of theoretical analysis our approach differs substantially from the mentioned prior work. We expand on this below:

- Discussion on [13]: To the best of our understanding, the current version of [13] provides an error bound on the learned conditional (posterior) distributions via the joint distributions. In Theorem 3, they show that under regularity assumptions, the learned posterior distributions converge if the joint distribution converges. However, we did not find an explicit discussion of the convergence of the learned conditional sampler or finite-sample error bounds. Although Section 3.2 informally argues that convergence of the gradient flows ensures the assumptions of Theorem 3 are satisfied, this still does not provide a finite-sample guarantee on the incurred loss.

- Discussion on CGMMD: In comparison we would like to highlight that our theoretical contribution not only establishes asymptotic convergence of the learned conditional distribution but also explicitly characterizes the finite-sample error. Moreover, as noted by the reviewer, our convergence analysis is carried out using an approximation class of neural networks similar to those considered in [5, 11, 14]. Also as pointed out by reviewer x7Ec our theoretical contribution has broader relevance with uses beyond this work, potentially benefiting other nonparametric or kernel-based generative models.

> Generally the optimal sampler g  is neither unique nor regular. Plenty of works show that the Lipschitz constant (and thus also the modulus of continuity) must explode whenever we approximate multimodal or heavy-tailed distributions, see e.g. [5,6]. In practice, the bound from Thm 4.1 will be very very loose. 

We agree with the reviewer that an optimal sampler may neither be regular nor unique. We first note that Theorem 4.1 and, more generally, Theorem E.1 provide finite-sample bounds on $L(\hat{\mathbf g})$. Although the Lipschitz constant may sometimes be difficult to control, this affects only the constants in the bound. Moreover, the assumptions under which these results hold are standard in the literature [5,10, 11,14], as also acknowledged by Reviewer B9NQ.

While Assumption 4.2 states that the true sampler $\bar{\mathbf g}$ is uniformly continuous, this is not essential. In fact, Theorem E.1 establishes that the bound on $L(\hat{\mathbf g})$ holds for any continuous conditional sampler $\bar{\mathbf g}$. Thus, whenever the true conditional distribution $P(Y \mid X)$ is ”nice”, we expect the existence of a “well-behaved” sampler with a small modulus of continuity, in which case non-uniqueness of the optimal sampler does not weaken the bound on $L(\hat{\mathbf g})$.

On the other hand, if the target conditional distribution is multimodal or heavy-tailed, then as shown in [12], enforcing smoothness on the sampler leads to an inflated modulus of continuity and therefore a potentially loose bound. However, Theorem E.1 states that the relevant term in the bound depends only on the modulus of continuity of $\bar{\mathbf g}$ restricted to a high-probability set $E$, which is often significantly smaller than the global modulus. Moreover, despite potential irregularities of the true sampler, the convergence guarantees in Corollary 4.1 and Corollary E.1 continue to hold. To the best of our understanding, this challenge is inherent to the problem itself rather than a limitation of our approach.

> Also, the notation is a bit confusing as the definition of \omega_g  skips one of the arguments of g (I guess it is the conditioning which is omitted here).

Thanks for the pointer. That was a typo, and we have fixed it in the revised manuscript.

comment.value:
> There is a significant mismatch between minimizing the MMD and its empirical estimators, in the sense that one needs a very large batch size in order to approximate the MMD precisely. Using a minibatch approximation usually yields blurred results which can be seen very well in Figure 2 where the CGMMD produces plenty of samples outside of the support of the target distribution compared to the baselines. A discussion on this topic is missing.

We appreciate the reviewer bringing this matter to our attention. For unconditional sampling, the role of batch size in MMD-based generative models has been well addressed in the literature, and typically large batch sizes are recommended. However, as in [15], an adversarial kernel could even work with low batch sizes yet produce good quality of generated samples. We believe that these same ideas can be also extended to conditional sampling. However, this is currently beyond the scope and goal of this particular paper, and we view this as a promising future work based on the foundational baseline that this paper sets up.

Additionally, we have now added a section on sensitivity analysis in the Appendix D where we study the influence of batch-size on the generation quality of CGMMD in the experimental setting of Section 5.1. With more batch sizes, the generation quality can be indeed improved a bit, especially in the tail region of the spiral. We demonstrate this by plotting the scatterplot of generated samples $(Y_1,Y_2)$ conditional on $X=1$, restricted to the regions $Y_1\le -0.5$ and $Y_2 \ge 3$ as we vary batch size in $\{200,400,600,800 \}$. As rightly pointed out by the reviewer, for small batch sizes, there were significantly more outliers, i.e., points far away from the center $(1,0)$. As the batch size increases, we indeed see a significant reduction in the number of these outliers in these two regions. However, the blurriness of the generated samples close to the center could not be addressed by simply increasing batch sizes, and are probably closely tied to multiple other factors, including the particular model architecture we take.

> Experiments: Compared to the literature, the paper only considers quite small experiments. I am not sure, whether denoising or superresolution tasks on MNIST really make sense as it is a really simplistic dataset. The quality of the results seems to be below classical image reconstruction methods like total variation. 

We appreciate the reviewer’s concerns. But, we would like to point out that beyond MNIST, we also evaluate our method on image denoising and image super-resolution using large-scale datasets such as CelebA (Section 5.2 and Appendix C.4) and STL10 (Appendix C.5). In the revised version, we additionally include an image inpainting experiment on FashionMNIST (Appendix C.6) to further illustrate the versatility of the CGMMD approach. While we acknowledge that the quality of these results may not yet match state-of-the-art benchmarks, our intention in this work is to establish a foundational framework for ECMMD-based one-shot conditional sampling, complemented by strong theoretical guarantees. We view our results as an initial step that demonstrates feasibility and motivates more optimized future developments that can truly compete with modern conditional generative models.


> Also, for this kind of task the evaluation of FID and inception score does not make sense, as they have a predefined ground truth and metrics like PSNR, SSIM or LPIPS can cover them much better (I noted that PSNR and SSIM are reported, but my point is that it doesn't really make sense to report FID and IS in this case). 

Thank you for the insightful comment. We agree that FID and IS are not appropriate metrics for tasks with known ground truth. We included them only to provide a direct comparison between CGMMD and the diffusion baseline, alongside the more relevant reconstruction metrics (PSNR and SSIM). We have removed the FID and IS columns from the results table.

> Given that the method matches the distributions of a generator with a data distribution, the authors should evaluate how much generative power their model has. Suitable tasks could be class conditional sampling or box-inpainting.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions. In the revised version of the manuscript, we have added an experiment on image inpainting with the FashionMNIST dataset (Appendix C.6), which further demonstrates the generative capabilities of our approach. Moreover, as previously included in Appendix D, we also provide class-conditional sampling results on the MNIST dataset, which highlight the same capability.

> I would prefer if the authors sharpened their Contributions section a bit to showcase what is new and what is taken from the literature. If I understand it correctly, the definition of the ECMMD and its empirical computation via neighborhood graphs comes from the literature, while the contribution in this paper is the construction of a conditional MMD GAN.

Indeed, the definition of ECMMD, and its empirical estimation are well-established in the literature, and we borrow this measure to the setting of conditional generative sampling to construct the CGMMD algorithm. In the camera-ready version, we will update the contribution section to clearly distinguish between them.

> Please state some relevant information about the experiments in Section 5. E.g. which kernel is used, which batch size etc.

In all our experiments, we use the Gaussian kernel and different batch sizes for different experiments. Now we have added the details to Section 5.

> Citations are not always accurate. For instance the fact that  almost surely iff  (line 97 to 101 and Lemma 2.1) is simply Bayes theorem and that the corresponding metrics are zero is an immediate consequence and existence of the mapping 
already follows from Breniers theorem; the citations in the paper are far away from being the origin of these results. Similarly, the form of the MMD in (2.2) exists for decades in the literature and attributing it to Chatterjee et al. is inaccurate.

We thank the reviewer for their careful reading of the draft and for pointing out the discrepancies in the references. We provide our detailed responses below.

We agree with the reviewer that it is immediately true that the metric is zero if and only if the conditional distributions are equal. However this result was formally shown in [6] and as a result we properly cited that proposition. 

We also agree that the existence of the mapping $\bar{\mathbf g}$ can be derived as a consequence of Brenier’s theorem. However, we would like to point out that Brenier’s theorem requires stronger assumptions than Lemma 2.1 (\textit{noise outsourcing lemma}). Moreover, we would like to highlight that the result in Lemma 2.1 is a well-known result in classical probability (see Theorem 5.10 from [1]) and is known by many names in the literature, including the \textit{noise outsourcing lemma} (see [2,3,4,5] and references within). We chose this convention because the particular version of the lemma stated in our work is taken from [5], which also refers to this lemma by this name. We have now acknowledged these previous works in the revised version. In addition, we have also added a comment about deriving Lemma 2.1 from Brenier’s theorem.

For the expression in equation (2.2), we would like to highlight that it is not exactly the same as the usual expression of MMD from [7]. While in the unconditional setting this expression corresponds to the classical definition of MMD and has indeed existed in the literature for a long time, the particular form used here has nuances in how the random variables are generated, specifically, the paired variables are generated conditional on the same $\mathbf X$. However, we agree that there are earlier references to the same result (for example, [8,9]), which we have now cited appropriately. We have also clarified the distinction between the unconditional and conditional variants in the updated draft.

Thanks for the replies and the updated paper.

Some of my comments are addressed (literature, inpainting task), for others I am still a bit sceptical/have questions regarding the authors reply:

> However, Theorem E.1 states that the relevant term in the bound depends only on the modulus of continuity of $\bar g$ restricted to a high-probability set $E$ than the global modulus. 

Can you make this precise? I am struggeling a bit to see this from Theorem E.1 (there $E$ is a cube with radius $R$, which is quite different from defining a high-density set).

> empirical estimators

Based on my experience, a batch size of 800 is still comparably small for getting a close approximation. In the setup of Appendix D I am not clear, which part of the error is due to constraints of the architecture and which part is due to the discretization error.

I think some simple statistics (which do not require retraining) could help here. E.g. compute the MMD used for training between
- generated points and target points with large batch size (much larger than in training)
- generated points and target points with the same batch size as for training
- two independent batches of target points with the same batch size as for training

If the second and third number approximately coincide, we know that the remaining error is mostly introduced by the approximation of the MMD with the empirical estimator. Also, I think that the choice of the kernel and the bandwidth have a crucial influence here.

Since you say that generation is cheap (and computing the MMD might not): Have you considered low-rank approximations of the MMD (like random Fourier features)?

> Experiments

I am still a bit unhappy about the inpainting/super-resolution examples with MNIST. For this kind of task, very simple baselines would do very well (the images are basically binary) and I do not think that those are the right examples for a conditional generative model. While I acknowledge that the authors only use comparably few computational resources (there is no problem with working with MNIST), I think other tasks (like the new inpainting one) or datasets (like the images one) which are already there in the appendix would be better suited for the main paper.

I also think that it is clear that (in the near future) this kind of MMD-GAN won't be competitive with diffusion-based methods or recent GANs in terms of quality (don't get me wrong, I do not think that this is really a problem, just an observation).

comment.value:
> Can you make this precise? I am struggling a bit to see this from Theorem E.1 (there $E$  is a cube with radius $R$, which is quite different from defining a high-density set).

Thanks for the question. You rightly pointed out that the theorem statement only mentions $E$ as a cube with radius $R$ and derives an upper bound on the error based on that. We would like to highlight that since the theorem statement holds true for any $R>0$, $E$ can be particularly chosen to be a high-probability region on the domain of $\bar{\mathbf{g}}$. To that end, observe that, using the independence of $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ and $\mathbf{X}$, 

$$
\mathbb{P}\big((\boldsymbol{\eta}, \mathbf{X}) \notin E\big)\ \le\ 1 - \Phi(R)^m  \mathbb{P} \left(\|\mathbf{X}\|_2 \le R\right).
$$

In the above equation, note that by choosing $R$ judiciously so that $\mathbf{X}$ has small mass beyond the $L_2$ ball of radius $R$, this term becomes small. This is indeed possible under our assumptions on the tails of $\mathbf{X}$, even allowing for a certain degree of heavy-tailed behavior. In particular, under our assumption E.2(2), this term reduces to the expression reported in Theorem E.1 (see also equation (E.6)). Informally, our argument is that, with an appropriately chosen $R$, $(\boldsymbol{\eta}, \mathbf{X})$ belongs to a set $E$ with high probability.

We also highlight that we make this specific choice of the set $E$ in order to directly apply the approximation results from [1]. However, it may be possible to keep the choice abstract and define $E$ as any high-probability set from the domain of $\bar{\mathbf{g}}$. Nevertheless, this does not change the main message: the bound depends on the modulus of continuity of $\bar{\mathbf{g}}$ when restricted to a high-probability subset of its domain, and thus can be well-behaved in a diverse set of practical settings. 

That being said, we acknowledge that this presents a trade-off when choosing $R$. However, under our assumptions, we can restrict $R$ to grow polynomially in $\log(1/\epsilon)$ (where $\epsilon$ controls the probability mass), with the precise growth depending on the heaviness of the tail behavior.

### References:

[1] Shen, Zuowei, Haizhao Yang, and Shijun Zhang. "Deep network approximation characterized by number of neurons." arXiv preprint arXiv:1906.05497 (2019).

We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. In the same experimental setting, after completing the training, we evaluate our model for batch size in ${400, 600, 800}$. Specifically, we compute the mean ECMMD distance (averaged over 50 iterations) between the generated and target samples, as well as between two independent sets of target samples. For both of these computations, we consider two batch sizes: (1) the training batch size and (2) a large batch size of $5000$. The corresponding results are summarized in the table below.
The true ECMMD distance between two independent target samples should ideally be zero. In practice, the reported values are approximately $10^{-4}$ for the large batch size, which is essentially the approximation error of the MMD estimator. When examining the ECMMD distances between the generated and target samples, we observe that increasing the batch size from the training batch size to the larger batch size has little impact on the ECMMD value. This further suggests that the dominant source of error possibly does not arise from the nearest neighbor-based approximation to MMD.

summary.value:
This paper introduces Conditional Generator using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (CGMMD), a new adversary-free framework for one-shot conditional sampling. The method trains a conditional generator $g(\eta,X)$ by minimizing the expected MMD between the conditional distribution and the model distribution.

The authors prove both the non-asymptotic finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic convergence of the learned conditional distribution to the true one in expected MMD.

Last, the authors provide empirical results on synthetic data and image tasks (denoising and super-resolution) demonstrate good performance and speedups over conditional diffusion models.

strengths.value:
1. **Bridging theory and practice**: the paper not only demonstrate the performance of the proposed CGMMD empirically, but also provide theoretical analysis on the loss convergence, deepening the theoretical understanding of the method.

2. **Broader relevance**: The analysis of nearest-neighbor-based concentration inequalities could be useful beyond this work, potentially benefiting other nonparametric or kernel-based generative models.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Limited comparison to diffusion-based models**: diffusion with CFG is one of the most popular conditional generation methods nowadays. I feel more comparison to it should be provided, especially on the generation quality and generation time on other larger-scale datasets.

2. **Lack of illustration on parameter setting in numerical experiments**: it is not clear how the parameters/kernels/$k_n$ are chosen in the experiments.

questions.value:
1. How does different kernels and $k_n$ affect the performance of CGMMD?

2. In the synthetic data experiments (Figure 2), CGMMD seems to tend to underestimate the variance and concentrate on the center. Does similar phenomenon happen in other experiments? Is there any intuition behind this kind of generation bias for CGMMD?

confidence.description: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

comment.value:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for their valuable time, constructive feedback, and positive evaluation. We are pleased that the reviewer recognizes both the empirical performance and the theoretical guarantees of our work, specifically highlighting the potential utility of the nearest-neighbor-based concentration inequality analysis beyond the scope of this paper. We address each of the reviewer's points in detail below.

> Limited comparison to diffusion-based models: diffusion with CFG is one of the most popular conditional generation methods nowadays. I feel more comparison to it should be provided, especially on the generation quality and generation time on other larger-scale datasets.

Thank you for the insightful suggestion. The primary goal of this work is to introduce CGMMD as an alternate approach to one-shot conditional sampling. We agree that modern diffusion models with classifier-free guidance provide a strong and widely used benchmark. However we would like to point out that our focus is not on competing with the state-of-the-art approaches like diffusion based methods but on establishing a theoretically solid approach to one shot conditional sampling with statistical guarantees on the convergence of the sampler. We would also like to point out that while a more comprehensive comparison with diffusion based methods can be built on top of the current work as future work, that will not affect the core claims of CGMMD. To clarify, we agree with the reviewer that CFG presents a well established benchmark and our intention is not to re-benchmark it, rather to convey the message that CGMMD achieves the intended effect with reduced inference time cost.


> Lack of illustration on parameter setting in numerical experiments: it is not clear how the parameters/kernels/$k_n$ are chosen in the experiments.

Thanks for the pointer. In the revised version, we have added details on some of these choices, like kernel and number of neighbors, etc in Appendix D. We remark that some of these choices are tuned to the particular experiment in hand. In all our experiments, we choose the Gaussian kernel (mentioned in Appendix C). 

> How does different kernels and $k_n$ affect the performance of CGMMD?

We experimented with other kernels, including linear and polynomial, but found that the Gaussian kernel offered the most reliable optimization with minimal hyperparameter tuning. We believe that the Gaussian kernel performed better because it yields stable gradients during training (as the kernel is bounded).

The $k$-NN graph is constructed within each mini-batch and recomputed every iteration. A smaller $k_n$ emphasizes very local conditional neighbourhoods, leading to lower bias but higher variance. Conversely, a larger $k_n$ results in smoother, lower-variance gradients but introduces higher bias. In our experiments, we selected $k_n$ as a fraction of the batch size $B$, specifically within the range $k_n/B \in [0.05, 0.20]$.

> In the synthetic data experiments (Figure 2), CGMMD seems to tend to underestimate the variance and concentrate on the center. Does similar phenomenon happen in other experiments? Is there any intuition behind this kind of generation bias for CGMMD?

That is an interesting observation. We agree that the conditional samples generated by CGMMD tend to concentrate around the center. However, we would like to point out that this phenomenon is not just tied to CGMMD, and the other competing methods, like GCDS and WGAN, also show a similar behavior. In fact, we believe that this behavior is tied to the particular experiment at hand. More precisely, under no noise ($\sigma=0$), the conditional samples truly form a spiral, while for non-trivial noises the true spiral structure near the center tends to get obscured and gets replaced by a mass (for e.g., see the right-most panels of Figure 2, especially for $\sigma=0.4,0.6$). This naturally tends to bias the generator towards the center, and can be seen to be depicted by all the methods considered in this experiment.

We also remark that we do not necessarily see the same behavior for other experiments. In particular, in Appendix C.1, we consider the synthetic simulation setting where the true conditional samples form a circular structure, and there we do not see any such bias, and the generated samples spread more uniformly.

**We hope we have addressed the concerns of the reviewer. If you believe this is not the case, please let us know so that we have a chance to respond.**

Our paper focuses on conditional sampling, specifically on learning and sampling from the conditional distribution $p(y|x)$. summary.value: The paper proposes CGMMD, a conditional generator trained by directly minimizing an Expected Conditional MMD (ECMMD) loss estimated with a k-nearest-neighbor graph over the conditioning variables. This yields a one-shot conditional sampler: draw noise $\eta$ and evaluate $\widehat{g}(\eta, x)$ in a single forward pass, avoiding adversarial training and diffusion’s iterative denoising. The authors give a finite-sample generalization bound for the learned sampler and a convergence result (in MMD and via characteristic functions). Experiments span synthetic helix-shaped conditionals and image tasks (MNIST super-resolution/denoising, CelebHQ denoising); compared with a conditional diffusion baseline, CGMMD is ~100× faster per image but with lower perceptual quality. Algorithmic details and the kNN ECMMD estimator are spelled out.

strengths.value:
- Clear objective, no min–max: Framing training as direct ECMMD minimization sidesteps GAN instability and mode collapse while preserving flexibility of neural generators.

- One-shot conditional sampling: Practical speed advantage versus diffusion; single forward pass at test time. Table shows orders-of-magnitude faster generation.

- Theory with modern tools: Non-asymptotic error bound and convergence guarantee; analysis combines uniform concentration for kNN functionals and NN approximation theory.

- Sound choice of discrepancy: ECMMD is a strict scoring rule for conditionals, grounding the objective in kernel mean embeddings. This aligns with prior work formalizing ECMMD. 

- Positioned in the literature: Connects thoughtfully to MMD foundations and conditional generative approaches (GAN/OT/diffusion).

weaknesses.value:
- Assumption load and scope: Theory requires sub-Gaussian X, uniqueness in kNN graphs, bounded Lipschitz characteristic kernels, and a nontrivial regularity condition on conditional mean embeddings. This is reasonable but limiting in heavy-tailed or structured-X regimes.

- Batching. How is the data being generated? In each epoch, do we get a fresh sample of $y$s? And how did you get kNNs to work on mini-batches?

- Estimator design choices left open: Performance will depend on kernel, bandwidth, and k; guidance for tuning/robustness and sensitivity analyses are minimal. (MMD performance is known to be kernel-dependent.) 

- Empirics are narrow: Image tasks are small-scale; diffusion outperforms on PSNR/SSIM/FID despite CGMMD’s speed, and baselines omit strong conditional flows/normalizing flows which are fairly common. 

- Scalability details: kNN graphs each batch add overhead and may complicate very large-scale or high-dimensional X; no discussion of approximate NN structures etc to accelerate ECMMD.

- Comparative framing: The diffusion baseline uses classifier-free guidance but lacks careful parity in compute/architecture; more apples-to-apples studies (e.g., distilled diffusion or faster samplers) would help.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and suggestions. We address the concerns of the reviewer below.

> Assumption load and scope: Theory requires sub-Gaussian X, uniqueness in kNN graphs, bounded Lipschitz characteristic kernels, and a nontrivial regularity condition on conditional mean embeddings. This is reasonable but limiting in heavy-tailed or structured-X regimes.

We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to our assumptions. **In Appendix E, we relax the assumptions stated in Section 4 of the main text.** Theorem E.1 provides a generalisation of Theorem 4.1 and establishes a finite-sample error bound under these weaker conditions. Specifically, the sub-Gaussian assumption can be relaxed to a heavier-tailed sub-Weibull condition (see equation (E.1) and [1]). As noted in Section 4, the uniqueness assumption on nearest neighbours can also be weakened by adopting tie-breaking schemes (e.g., Section 7.3 of [2]), though doing so introduces additional technical complications.

The boundedness condition on the kernels can similarly be relaxed to the finiteness of certain moments. We impose boundedness primarily for technical convenience, and **we note that this assumption is satisfied by commonly used kernels such as the Gaussian and Laplace kernels**. Likewise, the **Lipschitz assumption on the kernels is also satisfied by most standard kernels, including Gaussian and Laplace**. These Lipschitz conditions are required to obtain uniform concentration for non-linear statistics under nearest-neighbour-based weak interactions. While Lipschitzness can potentially be relaxed, the resulting bounds may involve seminorms on the underlying function classes (see [3,4]), which can limit practical applicability.

Finally, as emphasised in the main text, the regularity condition on the mean embeddings is our most critical assumption. Appendix~F discusses this in detail. In particular, we show that this assumption holds, for example, when the true conditional density is a smooth function of $\|x\|_2$ and when the density ratio between the conditional generators and the true density exhibits sufficiently regular behaviour.


> Batching. How is the data being generated? In each epoch, do we get a fresh sample of $y$s? And how did you get kNNs to work on mini-batches?

Thank you for the question. We follow Algorithm 1, as written in the paper. Before training, we pre‑generate all $\eta_i$​ and construct a dataset of triplets $(x_i, y_i, \eta_i)$, which are fed to the dataloader (i.e., no on‑the‑fly sampling during training). During training, each epoch makes a full pass over this dataset. At every iteration, we take a mini‑batch of size B (e.g., B=100 for MNIST super‑resolution) and build the k-NN graph within that mini‑batch only, i.e, we compute pairwise distances among the B examples and connect each example to its k nearest neighbours in the current batch. So, in each iteration, a fresh batch of $(y_i)$ is taken from the dataloader to construct the k-NN graph. We have included this detail in Section 3 of the revised version.

> Estimator design choices left open: Performance will depend on kernel, bandwidth, and k; guidance for tuning/robustness and sensitivity analyses are minimal. (MMD performance is known to be kernel-dependent.)

We understand the reviewer’s concern. We had a brief discussion on the choice of kernels in Appendix D, where we have discussed different choices of kernels as well as using multiple kernels for learning the generator (similar to [5]). In our experiments, we used the Gaussian kernel with bandwidth being $\sqrt{p}$, the dimension of $\mathbf{Y}$ (as suggested by [6]). To the best of our knowledge, the optimal choice of bandwidth for kernel-based methods is an open problem, while the median heuristic (see [7]) is a popular alternative in two-sample testing problems, it is not immediately clear on how to extend that for generative purposes and in the conditional setting. We have expanded our discussion of these design choices in Appendix D.

>  Empirics are narrow: Image tasks are small-scale; diffusion outperforms on PSNR/SSIM/FID despite CGMMD’s speed, and baselines omit strong conditional flows/normalizing flows which are fairly common.

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern. Regarding the comparison with diffusion models, we would like to clarify that we do not claim CGMMD outperforms diffusion models in terms of quality of the generated samples. The purpose of our experiment was to validate CGMMD and to demonstrate its improved speed while maintaining reasonable efficiency.

In Appendix C.2 of the revised manuscript, **we have also added comparisons with conditional/normalizing flows in simulated settings**, including (i) bivariate distributions supported on a lower-dimensional manifold (a circle) and (ii) the two-moons benchmarking task [8] commonly used in simulation-based inference. Our results are consistent with findings from previous work [9].

comment.value:
> Scalability details: kNN graphs each batch add overhead and may complicate very large-scale or high-dimensional X; no discussion of approximate NN structures etc to accelerate ECMMD.

That is a great question, and we understand the reviewer’s concern. First of all, we want to highlight that the main focus of the work is not to optimize the training time of the model **but to develop a method with reduced inference time**. 

Initially, it was taking a lot of time to compute the nearest neighbour graphs using the standard Python function sklearn.neighbors.kneighbors_graph. This function is written for the CPU and was the bottleneck when we were training the model on PyTorch using GPU. To accelerate the training, we wrote our own function to compute the kNN graph on the GPU, and this reduced the training time significantly. The order of computation of our implementation is $O(B^2)$, where B is the batch size in each sample. However, there are efficient ways of approximating the kNN graphs which require $O(B \log B)$ time. We have included these details between lines in Appendix D..

Regarding the reviewer’s concern about high-dimensional X: Real-world data are usually high-dimensional, but almost always reside on low-dimensional manifolds; leveraging such embeddings improves reconstruction quality, as also noted by prior works [10, 11, 12]. Therefore, for tackling the high-dimensional X, one can take an embedding into a lower dimension and fit the CGMMD model on the lower-dimensional data. For example, as discussed in Appendix C.5 containing the STL10 example, we embed the images into a lower-dimensional space via the ResNet18 encoder.
